title: Personality and Appearance

paragraphs.text: When 19th-century scientist Charles Darwin applied to accompany ship's captain Robert Fitzroy on his voyage, he was almost let down by his appearance. Fitzroy believed in physiognomy—the idea that you can tell a person's character from their appearance—and believed that Darwin's nose indicated laziness. This was hardly the case, but fortunately Darwin's forehead gave a more favourable impression and he was allowed onboard and could pursue his theory of evolution.

The idea that a person's character can be glimpsed in their face dates back to ancient Greece, and was popular in 18th-century intellectual circles. It was only after the subject became associated with phrenology, the belief that mental capacity could be evaluated by measuring the skull, that physiognomy was likewise written off as pseudoscience.

It's true, though, that within a tenth of a second of seeing an unfamiliar face we have already made a judgement about character. Once that judgement has formed, it is surprisingly hard to budge. Moreover, politicians with competent-looking faces have a greater chance of being elected, as do people aspiring to be CEOs. Furthermore, people seen as good-looking are judged to be more outgoing, intelligent and healthy. They are even treated better by the justice system.

Is there any substance to such judgements? In 1966, psychologists at the University of Michigan asked 84 strangers to rate each other on five personality traits, based on appearance, while sitting silently for 15 minutes. For three traits—extroversion, conscientiousness and openness—the observers' judgements matched real personality scores significantly more often than chance. More recently, researchers Anthony Little and David Perrett have re-examined the appearance-personality link. They pointed out the Michigan studies were not tightly controlled: the participants could have been swayed by posture and movement. But when they re-ran the experiment using photos, they did find a link, though only for extroversion and conscientiousness, indicating there was merely a correlation at the extremes of personality.

Justin Carré and Cheryl McCormick of Brock University in Ontario studied 90 ice-hockey players: they found wider faces, in which the cheekbone-to-cheekbone distance was unusually large relative to the distance between brow and lip, were linked in a statistically significant way with the number of penalty minutes a player received for violent acts. The critical question is whether people judge wider-faced men as more aggressive. Carré and McCormick are studying this, and though the results are not all in, they say a preliminary analysis suggests they do. It would mean men with high testosterone levels, who are known to be stronger and more dominant, tend to have rounder faces and that we evolved to judge these as aggressive because their owners are more likely to attack us.

However, Leslie Zebrowitz, psychologist at Brandeis University, says that in many cases snap judgements are inaccurate, stemming from our natural tendency to overgeneralize. An example of overgeneralisation can be seen in predators' response to eye spots, the circular markings on some butterflies. These act as a deterrent to predators because they mimic the eyes of other creatures which might be threatening.

Alexander Todorov of Princeton University recently put forward a theory which he says explains our judgements of faces in terms of how threatening they appear. He asked people for their reactions to pictures of emotionally neutral faces, and found two underlying factors: how trustworthy and dominant the face looks. He then worked out which aspects of facial appearance were associated with looking trustworthy, untrustworthy, dominant or submissive and created exaggerated computer portraits of people with these characteristics. An extremely untrustworthy face, for example, has the corners of the mouth curled down.

Todorov concludes personality judgements based on people's faces are an overgeneralisation of our evolved ability to infer emotions from facial expressions, and hence a person's intention to cause us harm. He stresses, too, that overgeneralisation still leaves room for the idea that there is sometimes some truth in these assessments, particularly in the case of dominance: He says, 'It is not the case that overgeneralisation and "kernel of truth" ideas are mutually exclusive.'

So if there is some truth, where does it come from? Perrett suspects the link arises when our prejudices about faces turn into self-fulfilling prophecies, maintaining that our expectations can lead us to influence people to behave in ways confirming those expectations: consistently treat someone as untrustworthy and they will behave accordingly.

This effect sometimes works the other way round, however, especially for the cute. Zebrowitz has found that baby-faced men stimulate an emotional centre of the brain, the amygdala, which provokes a nurturing response from people who interact with them. Perhaps surprisingly, it has also been found they are more likely to commit an offense. Zebrowitz has found baby-faced boys to be assertive too, and more likely to be academically successful, which she suggests may derive from their striving to confound other people's beliefs about them.

There is another theory that our personality moulds the way our faces look. It is convincingly backed up by a study which found that angry old people looked cross even when asked to strike neutral expressions. A lifetime of scowling has left its mark. In a way then, we get the face we deserve.
